2027-07-28.title: Saint Alphonsa of the Immaculate Conception, Virgin
readings: Moses did not know that the skin of his face shone because he had been talking with God
Holy is the Lord our God
In his joy he goes and sells all that he has and buys that field
2027-07-28.alt: Memorial in the calendar of the Church in India (verify the rank locally); the weekday readings of Week 17 (Year I) are used, and the prayers may be taken from the Common of Virgins. St Alphonsa died on 28 July 1946 and was canonised on 12 October 2008. Psalm verses are the same in NRSV and the Lectionary. Liturgical colour: white.
2027-07-28.verse: Moses came down from Mount Sinai. As he came down from the mountain with the two tablets of the covenant in his hand, Moses did not know that the skin of his face shone because he had been talking with God.
theo: Moses comes down Mount Sinai for the second time, with the new tablets in his hands, and he does not know that his face is shining. “Moses did not know that the skin of his face shone because he had been talking with God.” He has spent forty days in the presence of the Lord, and the glory has left its mark on him, though he himself is the last to notice. Aaron and the Israelites see it and are afraid to come near, so Moses calls them, speaks to them, and gives them the commands he has received; then he puts a veil over his face. Whenever he goes in to speak with the Lord he takes the veil off, and when he comes out he tells the people what he has been told, and they see again that his face is shining. The Psalm recalls this friendship: “Moses and Aaron were among his priests, Samuel also was among those who called on his name. They cried to the Lord, and he answered them. He spoke to them in the pillar of cloud.” The holiest people in Scripture are those who have been with God and do not realise how much of him they carry. St Paul will say that in Christ the veil is removed and that “all of us, with unveiled faces, seeing the glory of the Lord as though reflected in a mirror, are being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another” (2 Corinthians 3:18).

The Gospel gives two tiny parables, each of one sentence. A man finds a treasure hidden in a field, hides it again, and “in his joy he goes and sells all that he has and buys that field.” A merchant who knows pearls finds “one pearl of great value” and sells everything to buy it. Notice the word “joy.” Neither man calls it a sacrifice. They give up everything because they have found something better, and the finding comes first. This is how the Church understands the call to follow Christ, and the consecrated life in particular: not a loss but a discovery. St Paul says the same of himself: “whatever gains I had, these I have come to regard as loss because of Christ... because of the surpassing value of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord” (Philippians 3:7–8). The poor man with the field and the rich merchant show that the kingdom is for every kind of person, and that the price is the same for both: all that one has.

Today the Church in India keeps the memorial of a woman who found the pearl early and whose face shone without her knowing it. Alphonsa was born Anna, called Annakutty, on 19 August 1910 at Kudamaloor, near Kottayam in Kerala, into a Syro-Malabar Catholic family. Her mother died when she was small, and she grew up in the care of relatives. From childhood she wanted to belong wholly to Jesus. As a young girl, to avoid a marriage that others were arranging, she injured her feet in a fire, a rash act that the Church does not hold up for imitation, but which shows how single her desire was. She entered the convent of the Franciscan Clarist Congregation at Bharananganam in 1927, received the habit in 1928 and the name Alphonsa of the Immaculate Conception, and made her first vows in 1931 and her final vows in 1936. Her life was short and hidden, and full of illness. She taught young children for a time and could do little of the work that the world counts as important. Yet in her letters and in the memory of her sisters she appears as a woman who took her sufferings in union with the Cross of Christ, offered them for others, and met everyone with gentleness. She died at Bharananganam on 28 July 1946, aged thirty-five. Her tomb in the church of St Mary there became a place of pilgrimage. Pope St John Paul II beatified her at Kottayam on 8 February 1986, and Pope Benedict XVI canonised her in Rome on 12 October 2008: she is the first woman of Indian origin to be canonised and the first canonised saint of the Syro-Malabar Church. Like Moses, she did not know that her face was shining; the people of Kerala saw it and came near. Like the merchant, she found one pearl and sold everything. And like the grain of wheat of the Gospel, she fell into the earth and bore much fruit (John 12:24).
conn: The Hebrew verb is related to a word for “horn” or “ray.” St Jerome's Latin translation read “horned,” which is why Moses is painted and carved with horns, as in Michelangelo's statue. The Hebrew means he shone with rays of light.

Moses veiled his face after speaking with the people and unveiled it when he went into the Lord's presence. St Paul uses the image: in Christ, Christians look at the glory of the Lord “with unveiled faces” and are transformed (2 Corinthians 3:12–18).
Holiness both frightens and attracts. The saints are not distant; they are people through whom God's light is allowed to reach others.
Psalm 99 names three who called on the Lord and were answered: Moses, Aaron and Samuel. Intercessors who spoke with God are the Old Testament pattern of the saints who pray for us.

In a land without banks, people buried valuables in the ground and sometimes died without recovering them. Finding such a treasure in someone else's field was a stroke of fortune. The parable's point is not the finder's cleverness but his joy and the readiness to give all.
Pearls were among the most precious goods of the ancient world, traded across the seas from the Gulf and the Indian Ocean. A merchant who knew pearls could recognise one of great value at once.
A Syro-Malabar religious congregation of sisters following the Franciscan spirit, with its mother house in Kerala. Alphonsa joined its convent at Bharananganam in Kottayam district in 1927.
The name she took as a religious honours the doctrine, defined by Pope Pius IX in 1854, that Mary was preserved from original sin from the first moment of her conception (Catechism 490–493).
The first woman of Indian origin canonised.

St Alphonsa was canonised in St Peter's Square on 12 October 2008, together with three other saints. She is a daughter of the Syro-Malabar Church, an Eastern Catholic Church in full communion with Rome, and a saint honoured by the whole Church in India, whatever the rite.
altar: St Alphonsa lived her last years in pain, and she said that she offered it with the Cross of Jesus. This is what happens at every Mass. The one sacrifice of Calvary is made present on the altar, and we are invited to place on the paten our own struggles, illnesses and unseen sacrifices so that they are united to Christ's offering (Catechism 618, 1368). Nothing offered in love is wasted; the grain of wheat that dies bears fruit.

Moses came down with a shining face from speaking with God. After Holy Communion we too carry the Lord himself in our hearts, and, like Moses, we may not know that something of his light is on our faces. Let us go out from Mass as people who have been in his presence, and let others see it by our gentleness and joy.
outline: Ask: when did you last meet someone who had clearly been with God, and what did you notice about them?
Moses does not know his face shines; he veils it and unveils it before God.
Point 2 · The treasure and the pearl
The kingdom is found with joy, and the finder gives all.
Alphonsa's hidden suffering offered in love bears fruit in Kerala and the world.
The tomb at Bharananganam, with a line of pilgrims and a single lighted candle.
“Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains just a single grain; but if it dies, it bears much fruit.”
live: Choose one small pain, tiredness or disappointment today and offer it quietly to Jesus for someone by name, as St Alphonsa taught by her life.
Be gentle with someone who is hard to deal with this week, and let them see in you something of the peace you find in prayer.
Ask yourself what you would give up to follow Christ more fully, and take one step this week: a confession, a regular time of prayer, an act of generosity.
If you can, visit the tomb of St Alphonsa at Bharananganam or a church dedicated to her, or pray before her picture, asking her for the grace of patient love in suffering.
fathers: St Gregory the Great (Homilies on the Gospels 11, in substance)

The kingdom of heaven is a hidden treasure because it is the desire of heavenly things. One who has found it guards that desire and sells, that is, gives up, all earthly pleasures in order to buy the field of the Gospel life.
St Francis of Assisi (Canticle of the Creatures, in substance)
Praised be you, my Lord, through those who pardon for love of you, and who bear sickness and trial: blessed are those who endure in peace, for by you, Most High, they will be crowned.
St Thérèse of Lisieux (Story of a Soul, in substance)
A hidden life in a convent can be great: she offered every small act and every small suffering for others and for the Church, and trusted that the love given in secret would reach the whole world.
magis: All the faithful, in whatever state of life, are called to the fullness of Christian life and to the perfection of love; holiness is the vocation of all.
Christ gives suffering a new meaning: it can unite us with his redemptive passion, and he invites his disciples to take up their cross and follow him.
Consecrated virgins and religious give their whole lives to Christ, as a sign of the kingdom and a witness of love for the Church.
Jesus asks his disciples to prefer him to everything and everyone, and to renounce all for his sake and the Gospel.
By canonising some of the faithful, the Church recognises their power of the Spirit of holiness and sustains the hope of the faithful by giving them saints as models and intercessors.
saints: St Alphonsa of the Immaculate Conception (1910–1946)

Born Anna Muttathupadathu at Kudamaloor, Kottayam; a Franciscan Clarist sister of the Syro-Malabar Church at Bharananganam; a hidden life of prayer, teaching and long illness offered in love; died 28 July 1946, aged 35; beatified 8 February 1986; canonised 12 October 2008, the first woman of Indian origin to be canonised and the first canonised saint of the Syro-Malabar Church. Her tomb at Bharananganam is a place of pilgrimage.
29 Jul: Sts Martha, Mary and Lazarus (memorial). 30 Jul: St Peter Chrysologus (optional memorial). 31 Jul: St Ignatius of Loyola (memorial).
2027-07-28.prayer: Lord God, you hid the life of St Alphonsa in a quiet convent and let it shine on the whole Church in India. Through her prayers, grant that we too may find the pearl of great value, offer our sufferings in love for others, and carry your light with gentleness, so that those who see us may come near and give glory to you. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, for ever and ever. Amen. St Alphonsa, pray for us.

quick: Moses comes down Sinai with a shining face, and does not know it; he veils it and unveils it before the Lord.
Jesus compares the kingdom to a treasure hidden in a field and a pearl of great value: the finder joyfully sells all.
St Alphonsa, a hidden Clarist sister of Kerala who offered her sufferings in love, is the first woman of Indian origin canonised.
catechism: How can suffering unite us with Christ?
Why does the Church canonise saints?
kidsaint: Alphonsa's first name was Annakutty, and she lived in Kerala. Her mother died when she was little, and she grew up loving Jesus very much. When she was older she became a sister in a convent at Bharananganam and was given the name Alphonsa. She was often sick, and sometimes she was in pain, but she never complained. She offered her pain to Jesus for other people, and she was kind to everyone. When she died in 1946 she was only thirty-five. Many people pray at her tomb, and in 2008 the Pope declared her a saint. She is the first woman from India to be made a saint. Lesson: even small, quiet things done with love for Jesus shine like light.
2027-07-28.special: Memorial of St Alphonsa (India): weekday readings of Week 17; first woman of Indian origin to be canonised (12 October 2008).
term: The solemn act by which the Pope declares that a deceased member of the faithful lived heroic holiness, is in heaven with God, and may be honoured by the whole Church as a saint and invoked as an intercessor. The process normally goes through the titles Servant of God, Venerable, Blessed (beatification, usually after one miracle through the person's intercession) and Saint (canonisation, usually after a second miracle) (Catechism 828).

family.explain: Jesus tells a short story: a man found a treasure in a field. He was so happy that he sold everything he had and bought the field. Jesus is the greatest treasure of all. St Alphonsa loved Jesus so much that she gave her whole life to him. Even when she was ill and in pain, she smiled and was kind, and she prayed for other people. Today she is a saint, and we can ask her to pray for us.
family.intention: We pray for the sick and for people who are in pain, and we thank God for St Alphonsa.
family.ask: Ask: “What is the best thing that we have found in our family? How can we show Jesus' light to others this week?”

illus: A schoolteacher from a village near Pala went to Bharananganam every year on the day before the new school year began. She would light a candle at the tomb of St Alphonsa, and standing there she would say a short prayer for each child in her class by name, naming the quiet ones twice. She said she was not asking for results in examinations; she asked for the grace to be patient. When she retired, a former pupil told her: I always knew that someone was praying for me. She had never once told them about the candle. (An illustrative story.)

pm.open: Lord Jesus, you are the treasure and the pearl. Make us joyful finders, ready to give all, and let our hidden lives shine with your light. Amen.
share: Moses did not know that the skin of his face shone (Exodus 34:29). What might others see in me that I do not see?
He goes and sells all that he has and buys that field (Matthew 13:44). What is the treasure that I have found, and what is it asking of me?
Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies (John 12:24). What hidden suffering of mine could be offered for others?
pm.resp: Holy is the Lord our God.
interc: For the Church in India, in all her rites, that she may honour her saints and live the Gospel with joy.
For the Franciscan Clarist sisters and all religious women, that their hidden lives may bear fruit for the Church.
For the sick, especially those in long illness, that they may find in St Alphonsa a friend and be united with Christ's passion.
For young people discerning a vocation, that they may find the pearl and be generous.
For our group, that we may carry the light of Christ gently into our homes and work.
pm.close: God of holiness, you make your glory shine in the lives of your saints. By the prayers of St Alphonsa, make us treasure Christ above all things. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

homily: Dear brothers and sisters, there is something very beautiful about a face that has been in the presence of God. Moses comes down the mountain, and his face is shining. And the Bible says: Moses did not know that the skin of his face shone because he had been talking with God (Exodus 34:29). The people could see it, but he could not. Holiness is like that. It does not know itself.

Today the Church in India remembers a woman whose face shone like that. Annakutty was born in 1910 in a village near Kottayam. Her mother died when she was small. She grew up wanting to belong to Jesus, and in 1927 she entered the convent of the Clarist sisters at Bharananganam. She took the name Alphonsa of the Immaculate Conception. She was never strong. She was often ill, and she could do little of what the world calls important. She died at thirty-five. And the people of Kerala came to her tomb, and the Church has called her a saint.

What was her secret? The Gospel today gives us the answer: the treasure and the pearl. A man finds a treasure in a field, and in his joy he goes and sells all that he has and buys that field (Matthew 13:44). In his joy: that is the key. Alphonsa did not give up everything out of sadness. She had found Jesus, and he was worth more than anything else. St Paul says the same: I regard everything as loss because of the surpassing value of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord (Philippians 3:8).

And she gave her suffering a meaning. She offered her pain, in union with the Cross of Christ, for others. The Lord himself says: unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains just a single grain; but if it dies, it bears much fruit (John 12:24). Alphonsa's life was like a grain in the earth, hidden, small, and falling. And look at the harvest: pilgrims at her tomb, sick people finding peace, young women hearing the call, a whole Church in India rejoicing, and the Pope in Rome calling her a saint in 2008.

What about us? Perhaps we feel that our lives are small and hidden, with nothing great to show. But this is exactly where holiness grows. Let us offer our small pains and ordinary duties with love. Let us look for the pearl. And let us be gentle, because, like Moses, we may be carrying a light we do not see. St Alphonsa, pray for us. Amen.
kids: Children, today we remember St Alphonsa, who lived in Kerala. Her name when she was little was Annakutty. She loved Jesus very much, and she became a sister. She was often ill, but she was never cross; she offered her pain to Jesus for other people. When she died, people started praying at her grave, and the Pope said she is a saint. She is the first woman from India to be made a saint! Jesus said that heaven is like a treasure in a field. Alphonsa found the treasure. Who is the treasure? Jesus! Let us try to be kind today, even if we are tired, and offer it to him.

intro: Theme: “Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains just a single grain; but if it dies, it bears much fruit.”
A shining face, a pearl of great value and a hidden life: St Alphonsa shows what happens when a person finds the treasure.

points.apply: Give some time each day this week to be quietly with the Lord, and let the light of that time reach someone else.

sub: A hidden life of illness and prayer.
q: May those who sow in tears reap with shouts of joy. Those who go out weeping, bearing the seed for sowing, shall come home with shouts of joy, carrying their sheaves.

concl: Moses shows that those who speak with God carry his light, and that the saints are people through whom it reaches others.
St Alphonsa found the pearl, gave all, and offered her hidden sufferings for others, so that her life, like the grain of wheat, bears much fruit in Kerala and the world.
2027-07-28.resolve: Offer one hidden difficulty each day this week for someone by name, and be gentle with one person who tries your patience.
